title: Rate limiting
summary: Protect a boundary with a limiter; pick the algorithm from the burst you allow.

parts.rule: A rate limiter protects a boundary by counting work against a key such as user, tenant, API token, account, or IP address. Choose the algorithm from the allowed burst shape: token bucket allows a bounded burst and steady refill; leaky bucket smooths output; sliding windows give a more accurate recent count than fixed windows. Exceeded HTTP requests should receive 429 and useful retry information.
parts.why: A single client can exhaust shared CPU, database connections, or an expensive third-party quota. A poorly keyed limiter can also punish innocent users, and a fixed-window edge can allow twice the intended burst. The design must state where decisions run, how distributed instances share counters, and what happens if the limiter store is unavailable.
parts.example: A public short-link API allows 100 creates per hour per API key but tolerates a short burst of 20. Use a token bucket with capacity 20 and a refill of one token every 36 seconds. A full bucket accepts 20 immediate creates; after that, another request succeeds only as tokens return. Each gateway performs an atomic read-refill-consume update in a shared store keyed by create:{apiKey}, so two gateways cannot spend the same last token. When empty, return 429 with Retry-After based on the next refill, not a silent timeout. Separate buckets can protect the whole tenant and the individual key so 50 keys cannot bypass the tenant's purchased quota. Login needs different fairness and security: combine a per-account limit with a coarser per-IP signal, because IP-only blocking hurts offices and carrier networks while account-only limiting lets an attacker rotate usernames. A sliding window of 5 failed attempts in 15 minutes avoids the sharp reset of a fixed window. Decide outage behavior by risk: a read-only public endpoint may fail open with a local emergency cap, while password attempts or costly writes may fail closed briefly. Track allowed and rejected counts so the limit can be tuned from evidence.
parts.use: Rate-limit authentication, public APIs, expensive searches, writes, and calls backed by scarce quotas. Key the limiter to the entity that should receive a fair share, layer local and global protection when necessary, and document burst capacity, sustained rate, response headers, and outage policy.
parts.refuse: Do not use one global counter that lets one heavy tenant block everyone. Avoid IP as the only identity when many users share addresses. Do not silently drop requests or apply the same limit to a cached read and an expensive export. A complex distributed limiter is unnecessary when one gateway and an in-memory bucket already meet the current scale.

body:
Rule. A rate limiter protects a boundary by counting work against a key such as user, tenant, API token, account, or IP address. Choose the algorithm from the allowed burst shape: token bucket allows a bounded burst and steady refill; leaky bucket smooths output; sliding windows give a more accurate recent count than fixed windows. Exceeded HTTP requests should receive 429 and useful retry information.

Why it matters. A single client can exhaust shared CPU, database connections, or an expensive third-party quota. A poorly keyed limiter can also punish innocent users, and a fixed-window edge can allow twice the intended burst. The design must state where decisions run, how distributed instances share counters, and what happens if the limiter store is unavailable.

Worked example. A public short-link API allows 100 creates per hour per API key but tolerates a short burst of 20. Use a token bucket with capacity 20 and a refill of one token every 36 seconds. A full bucket accepts 20 immediate creates; after that, another request succeeds only as tokens return. Each gateway performs an atomic read-refill-consume update in a shared store keyed by create:{apiKey}, so two gateways cannot spend the same last token. When empty, return 429 with Retry-After based on the next refill, not a silent timeout. Separate buckets can protect the whole tenant and the individual key so 50 keys cannot bypass the tenant's purchased quota. Login needs different fairness and security: combine a per-account limit with a coarser per-IP signal, because IP-only blocking hurts offices and carrier networks while account-only limiting lets an attacker rotate usernames. A sliding window of 5 failed attempts in 15 minutes avoids the sharp reset of a fixed window. Decide outage behavior by risk: a read-only public endpoint may fail open with a local emergency cap, while password attempts or costly writes may fail closed briefly. Track allowed and rejected counts so the limit can be tuned from evidence.

[[diagram:token-bucket]]

When to use. Rate-limit authentication, public APIs, expensive searches, writes, and calls backed by scarce quotas. Key the limiter to the entity that should receive a fair share, layer local and global protection when necessary, and document burst capacity, sustained rate, response headers, and outage policy.

When to refuse. Do not use one global counter that lets one heavy tenant block everyone. Avoid IP as the only identity when many users share addresses. Do not silently drop requests or apply the same limit to a cached read and an expensive export. A complex distributed limiter is unnecessary when one gateway and an in-memory bucket already meet the current scale.
